title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
content:
Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.
The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.
Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

report.summary: Corma raised a $125M Series A at a $1B valuation just three months after launch, betting AI agents can defend against AI-accelerated cyberattacks.
report.background: Cybersecurity has become one of the fastest-moving AI application markets. Attackers are using automation and generative AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster, while defenders are under pressure to detect and respond in minutes. Corma emerged from stealth in August with AI models and agents trained for cyber defense. Its fundraising accelerated after October 21, when a critical PHP flaw, a Node.js flaw, a security incident at LiteLLM, and other disclosures hit at once—an example of the kind of multi-front security event that stresses security teams. Investors including NEA, Sequoia, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue have now committed $185 million total. The round reflects both fear of AI-accelerated attacks and belief that frontier AI research can be applied to protection, not just offense.
key_points: Corma raised $125 million in a Series A led by NEA at a $1 billion valuation, only about three months after launching its product. Total funding is now $185 million, with Sequoia, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue also backing the company. That pace shows how aggressively investors are chasing AI security startups.

The fundraise followed a chaotic October 21 for security teams: a critical flaw in PHP, a flaw in Node.js, a breach at LiteLLM, and other incidents were disclosed the same day. Corma's momentum illustrates how real-world attack waves can quickly turn AI defense from a nice-to-have into an urgent budget priority.

Corma builds AI models and agents trained specifically for cyber defense. It positions itself as a frontier AI research lab focused on protection, rather than a generic security vendor bolting on AI. That research-lab framing is central to its pitch to investors and CISOs.

Competition is intense. Kevin Mandia's Armadin, Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and many startups are also applying AI to security. Corma argues the market is young and large enough for multiple winners, but differentiation will depend on proof that its agents catch and respond to threats better than rivals.
report.impact: The deal signals that AI security is becoming a standalone venture category, not just a feature inside existing security platforms. For the AI industry, it validates the idea that frontier-model research can be commercialized for defense, and it will likely pull more talent and capital into AI red-teaming, detection, and automated response. For developers, expect more AI agents scanning code, dependencies, and cloud configurations—and more pressure to secure open-source components like PHP, Node.js, and LiteLLM before flaws become exploits. For regular users, the upside is faster patching and breach detection; the risk is overreliance on automated agents that can misfire or be attacked themselves. The real test is whether Corma's $1B valuation translates into fewer damaging incidents, not just faster funding rounds.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch Corma and Armadin, plus AI-security offerings from Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI. For hands-on testing, try open-source tools such as OWASP ZAP and Semgrep for application security, Trivy for container and dependency scanning, and Garak or PyRIT for LLM red-teaming. LiteLLM is widely used for routing across model providers, but its recent incident is a reminder to audit proxy and gateway security before deploying AI agents.
